newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's beaches under serious threat - report.
newsitem.headline: Australia's beaches under serious threat - report.

text.p: Australia's beaches are under serious threat from billions of litres of raw sewage, storm-water pollution such as heavy metals, animal faeces and litter, acccording to a survey of 1,612 beaches.

More than three billion litres (660 million gallons) of sewage is poured from 141 public sewerage outfalls into the ocean daily, according to the Human Impact on Australian Beaches report by the Surfrider Foundation of Australia.

The survey released on Tuesday found one in five sewerage outfalls discharge effluent that has received only primary treatment -- meaning that is has merely been allowed to settle in tanks before being pumped into the ocean.
The survey was conducted between February and June 1995 by 70 conservation groups, surfers and fishermen.

The survey found one quarter of Australia's estimated 7,259 beaches had stormwater pipes which after rain dump directly onto the beach rubbish such as used syringes, as well as heavy metals from road surfaces, pesticides from gardens and animal faeces.
The survey found 80 percent of beaches, which included remote beaches as well as those in urban areas, were strewn with litter such as food wrappers, plastic bags and cigarette butts.
Yet only half the beaches had garbage bins.
Of Sydney's 40-odd beaches, syringes were found on almost a quarter of them, including the city's most famous stretch of sand at Bondi Beach.
One in 20 beaches had lost their sand dunes due to beach front development, while 72 percent had buildings, roads or carparks within 250 metres (820 feet) of the high tide mark.

The Gold Coast strip of beaches in Queensland state, one of Australia's biggest tourist attractions, has lost its dune buffer, forcing local government to spend A$30 million (US$24 million) on sand replenishment programmes since the early 1970s.
A further A$53 million has been allocated for further sand retention work. Sand mining has also degraded one in 50 beaches.

"The results indicate that the coastline is under immense pressure from human impacts of every nature," said the report's author Michael Legge-Wilkinson. "But we're not pointing the finger at anyone. We all have a role to play."

The Surfriders Foundation of Australia was formed in 1991 as a lobby group for the country's two million surfers, focusing on environmental protection of beaches along Australia's 18,000-km (11,200-mile) coastline.

The report said that since Australia was colonised in 1788, population and economic growth has focused on the coastal zone, resulting in about 86 percent of Australia's 18 million population now living on the coast.
This compares with a global average of 60 percent.

"If Australia is to achieve ecologically sustainable development in the coastal zone, it must recognise these impacts and seek, in future coastal developments, to avoid some of the mistakes that have been made in the past," the report said.

Legge-Wilkinson said the survey found large areas of the Australian coastline showing little sign of human impact other than litter pollution, but added that a national coastal management plan was needed to protect what was left.
"We're continuing to develop our coastal zone and we're losing coastal habitat at an alarming rate. Anything we don't set aside now may be lost," he said.
